catalog_quote: 5.1.1. Структура слога: V, CV, VC, VCV. Ударение в Р.я. падает на начальный слог, что привело к сокращению трехсложных слов до двусложных. Образовавшиеся в результате этого процесса сочетания согласных, в свою очередь, часто подвергаются ассимиляции: *[báriʃa] > *[báirʃa] > bayśa [baiʃa] > [bɐiʃʲɛ] ‛сезон дождей’. Это стяжение, видимо, связано с i-метатезой, которая встречается также в некоторых двусложных словах: *[rati] > *[rait] > ayt [ait] ‛ночь’; *[kʰali] ‛пустой’ > khayl [kʰail] ‛пещера’. [Translation: 5.1.1. Syllable structure: V, CV, VC, VCV. Stress in R[ajbanshi/Kamta] falls on the initial syllable, which has led to the reduction of trisyllabic words to disyllables. The consonant clusters that arose through this process are in turn often subject to assimilation: *[báriʃa] > *[báirʃa] > bayśa [baiʃa] > [bɐiʃʲɛ] 'rainy season'. This contraction is apparently connected with i-metathesis, which also occurs in some disyllabic words: *[rati] > *[rait] > ayt [ait] 'night'; *[kʰali] 'empty' > khayl [kʰail] 'cave'.] (Toulmin 2011: 432-433). Supporting (Toulmin 2009: 94): 'This change is connected to the initial stress which characterises some KRDS lects, and is shared also with SCB. ... It is curious that in BN and SH, where there is no strong initial stress, *ɔ has /o/ as an irregular reflex in the first syllable of the word.'
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the initial syllable ('strong initial stress') in the Rangpur (RP), Thakurgaon (TH) and Bhatibari (BH) Kamta lects, as in Standard Colloquial Bangla; the Shalkumar (SH, Cooch Behar/Jalpaiguri) and Bongaigaon (BN, Assam) lects are said to lack strong initial stress. The author states that the synchronic conditioning of stress in these lects has not been studied.
new_statements.exceptions: SH (Shalkumar) and BN (Bongaigaon) lects have 'no strong initial stress'; no alternative stress position is given for them.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement made in passing while explaining a diachronic vowel-raising rule in non-initial (unstressed) syllables; word-level, based on the author's fieldwork at eight KRDS sites; no dedicated stress section, no citation-form vs phrase distinction.
new_statements.identity_note: Toulmin's statement is site-specific within rang1265 (his 'central + eastern KRDS'): strong initial stress at Rangpur (RP, Bangladesh), Thakurgaon (TH, Bangladesh) and Bhatibari (BH, West Bengal); 'no strong initial stress' at Shalkumar (SH, Cooch Behar/Jalpaiguri, West Bengal) and Bongaigaon (BN, Assam = Goalpariya area). Wilde 2008's initial-stress statement concerns Rajbanshi of Jhapa/Morang, Nepal (western KRDS = rajb1243), not this glottocode. Glottolog rang1265 subsumes Rangpuri, Kamta/Kamtapuri, Koch Rajbanshi and Goalparia.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing statement (Toulmin 2009, initial stress in KRDS lects) and a cleaner, dedicated statement of it: a one-sentence rule with a diachronic consequence rather than a passing remark inside a vowel-raising discussion. This is the best citation for initial stress in this language.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is on the first syllable; the sketch treats it as fixed and uses it to explain the historical loss of medial syllables (three-syllable words becoming two-syllable) and vowel-raising in non-initial syllables (sec. 5.1.2 refers back to 5.1.1 for the raising processes).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The sketch describes the Koch Bihar (Cooch Behar) variety (sec. 1.0, p. 430) and says the Bongaigaon variety is phonologically very close to Assamese (p. 433-434) without commenting on its stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Toulmin 2011 describes the Rajbanshi/Kamta of Koch Bihar (Cooch Behar) district, West Bengal, which it says is very similar to the varieties of Jalpaiguri, Dhubri (Assam) and Rangpur, Lalmonirhat and Nilphamari (Bangladesh); it explicitly excludes Surjapuri (Kishanganj, Bihar) and the Nepal Rajbanshi of Jhapa/Morang (= rajb1243, covered by a separate chapter by Poudel and Yadav). Toulmin 2006 compares eight KRNB lects (Kishanganj KS, Thakurgaon TH, Rangpur RP, Shalkumar SH, Bhatibari BH, Bongaigaon BN, plus two others) and its initial-stress remark applies to RP, TH, BH (and variably SH), not to BN.

new_statements.quote: It has been stated above that *o is rare in non-initial positions. However, the sound [o] has become very common in these positions in some lects through raising of *ɔ. This change is connected to the initial stress which characterises some KRNB lects, and is common also with SCB. [...] As noted above, the raising of non-initial *ɔ is related to the initial stress pattern found in these lects, and is termed "prosodic vowel raising". It is curious that in BN and SH, where there is no strong initial stress, *ɔ has /o/ as an irregular reflex in the first syllable of the word. [p. 140:] testing this hypothesis requires closer synchronic study of the conditioning of stress in KRNB lects than has been undertaken to date.

It is curious that in BN and SH,'; page 59 (footer 133) continues 'where there is no strong initial stress, *ɔ has /o/ as an irregular reflex in the first syllable of the word.' Te…
new_statements.relation_note: Same passage as the existing 2009 statement (the book is the revised thesis; the wording differs only in KRNB vs KRDS and 'common also with' vs 'shared also with'), so it agrees on initial stress for the Rangpur/Thakurgaon/Bhatibari core, and adds the qualification that the eastern (Bongaigaon) and Shalkumar lects lack strong initial stress. It adds nothing beyond the 2009 book already in the catalog.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No dedicated stress section. In passing, initial stress is said to characterise some KRNB lects (the ones with prosodic raising of non-initial *ɔ: Rangpur RP, Thakurgaon TH, Bhatibari BH, variably Shalkumar SH), while Bongaigaon (BN) and Shalkumar (SH) are said to lack strong initial stress; the author adds that the conditioning of stress in KRNB lects has not yet been studied synchronically. Ch. 7 (p. 298) only relays Kakati's contrast between Assamese penultimate stress and Bengali initial stress, about the neighbouring languages.
new_statements.exceptions: Lect-level variation: 'in BN and SH, where there is no strong initial stress' (Bongaigaon in Assam, Shalkumar in Jalpaiguri); the author explicitly states that stress conditioning in KRNB has not been studied. Chapters 3, 5, 6, 8 and appendices A-D contain no stress or accent statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Toulmin 2011 describes the Rajbanshi/Kamta of Koch Bihar (Cooch Behar) district, West Bengal, which it says is very similar to the varieties of Jalpaiguri, Dhubri (Assam) and Rangpur, Lalmonirhat and Nilphamari (Bangladesh); it explicitly excludes Surjapuri (Kishanganj, Bihar) and the Nepal Rajbanshi of Jhapa/Morang (= rajb1243, covered by a separate chapter by Poudel and Yadav). Toulmin 2006 compares eight KRNB lects (Kishanganj KS, Thakurgaon TH, Rangpur RP, Shalkumar SH, Bhatibari BH, Bongaigaon BN, plus two others) and its initial-stress remark applies to RP, TH, BH (and variably SH), not to BN.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on placement: both works (and the 2009 book already cited) put stress on the initial syllable. The only tension is in scope: Toulmin 2011 states initial stress as a flat rule for the Cooch Behar variety, while Toulmin 2006 (like 2009) hedges that initial stress "characterises some KRNB lects" and that Bongaigaon (Assam) and Shalkumar (Jalpaiguri) have "no strong initial stress", with the conditioning of stress unstudied. The catalog's fixed: initial syllable reading stands for the central lects (Cooch Behar, Rangpur, Thakurgaon, Bhatibari); the eastern Bongaigaon/Goalpara varieties, which shade into Assamese, may differ and are not described for stress anywhere in the opened sources.
